## Packages we will use

Packages are collections of useful functions, data and documentation written by other people as an extension of basic R features.

```{r packages}
# a collection of R packages including ggplot, lubridate, forcats, stringr, tidyr, dplyr
#install.packages("tidyverse")
library(tidyverse)
#additional package that sets the working directory
#install.packages("here")
library(here)
#additional package to change the scales on a time series plot
#install.packages("scales")
library(scales)
#additional package to calculate statistical significance
#install.packages("ggpubr")
#install.packages("tidyverse")
library(ggpubr)
#we will use this to save out the results as a PDF
#tinytex::install_tinytex()
```

##Section 1: Loading in the dataset

We will load in the data from the Bitsikas et al paper into a variable called fish_df. This is a subset of the total data and contains all the observations from the month of August.

```{r Section 1.1}
fish_df <- read.csv(file = here("zebrafish_behaviour_subset.csv"))

str(fish_df)
```

We can see that this is a dataframe that contains the 869, 486 observations or rows.

Each observation has a timepoint (time column), the distance travelled in 6 seconds (Dist_6s column), the genotype of the individual (genotype column), if the observation occured at day or night (daytime column) and the sleep-wake state of the individual (state column).

```{r Section 1.2}
#look at the first 6 rows
head(fish_df)
```

## Section 2: Convert format of date-time column

We will convert the time column to a date-time object using the function as_datetime() from lubridate.

We can also use the day(), hour() and minute() functions to extract the day, hour and minute from the time.

```{r Section 2.1}
fish_df$time <- as_datetime(fish_df$time)

fish_df$day <- day(fish_df$time)

fish_df$hour <- hour(fish_df$time)

fish_df$minute <- minute(fish_df$time)
```

For the first plot, we will filter for just the wildtype (WT) data using the filter() function. We will call the subset dataframe fish_WT. This subsets the dataframe from 869,486 rows to 263,682 rows.

```{r Section 2.2}
fish_WT <- filter(fish_df, genotype == "WT")
```

## Section 3: Plotting the time series

The function ggplot allows us to create a customizable data visualizations It requires the data to plot as the first variable, and the aesthetics to be used when making the plot (typically this is the x and y coordinates). You can then specify the type of plot you want to make with additional mapping layers. Here we use geom_line() but we will go through other examples of plots supported by ggplot.

```{r Section 3.1}
#plot the raw observations (264k observations) from fish_WT
#set the x axis to be time and the y axis to be distance moved in 6s
time_series_plot <- ggplot(data = fish_WT, mapping = aes(x = ___, y = Dist_6s)) + geom_line() 

time_series_plot <- time_series_plot + ggtitle("Plot 1: Zerbafish time series over 4 days")

time_series_plot
```

We can look at the data from one day of observations. By using the pipe operator %\>% we can run this in one line. The pipe operator takes the output of one function and passes it to be the input of a second function and so on. First we pass the fish_WT dataframe to the filter() function and then pass the result of this (the filtered dataframe) to ggplot and create the same time series plot as above.

```{r Section 3.2}
#plot all observations for one day
single_day_plot <- fish_WT %>% filter(day == 12) %>% ggplot(., aes(x = time, y = Dist_6s))

single_day_plot <- single_day_plot + annotate("rect", xmin = as_datetime("2022-08-12 00:00:00"), xmax = as_datetime("2022-08-12 09:00:00"), ymin = 0, ymax = 7,  fill = "grey", alpha = 0.6)  + annotate("rect", xmin = as_datetime("2022-08-12 22:00:00"), xmax = as_datetime("2022-08-12 23:59:59"), ymin = 0, ymax = 7,  fill = "grey", alpha = 0.6) 

single_day_plot <- single_day_plot + geom_line()

single_day_plot <- single_day_plot + scale_x_datetime(breaks = date_breaks(___))

single_day_plot <- single_day_plot + theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90)) 

single_day_plot <- single_day_plot + ggtitle("Plot 2: Zebrafish time series data over one day")

single_day_plot
```

We can compare this to the time series figure from the paper. We can see on both days there is more activity during the ___ and less at ___.

![](zebrafish_figure_1_edited.png)

## Section 4: Determining sleep vs wake

Distance moved over time (speed) at any given time point is used to make calls on if a fish is asleep or awake. We can find what the cutoff they used is by looking at what the minimum speed they call wake is and what the maximum speed they call sleep is.

```{r Section 4.1}
fish_wake <- fish_df %>% filter(state == "Wake") 
min(fish_wake$Dist_6s)

fish_sleep <- fish_df %>% filter(state == "Sleep") 
max(fish_sleep$Dist_6s)
```

It appears the cutoff they use is ___. We can see this cutoff when we plot the raw data as well.

```{r Section 4.2}
speed_plot <- ggplot(fish_WT, aes(x = time, y = Dist_6s, colour = ___)) + geom_line()

speed_plot <- speed_plot + scale_colour_manual(values = c("lightseagreen" , "navy"))
speed_plot <- speed_plot + ggtitle("Plot 3: Zebrafish sleep vs wake speed over time") 

speed_plot
```

And when we plot the speed for each sleep and wake observation.

```{r Section 4.3}
sleep_wake_plot <- fish_WT %>% filter(day == 10) %>% ggplot(., aes(y = Dist_6s, x = state, colour = state)) + geom_jitter(alpha = 0.2)

sleep_wake_plot <- sleep_wake_plot + annotate("segment", x = 0.5, xend = 2.5, y = ___, yend = ___,linewidth = 2, colour = "red") 

sleep_wake_plot <- sleep_wake_plot + scale_colour_manual(values = c("lightseagreen" , "navy")) 

sleep_wake_plot <- sleep_wake_plot + ggtitle("Plot 4: Zebrafish sleep vs wake cutoffs") 

sleep_wake_plot
```

## Section 5: Sleep timing in wildtype zebrafish

Zebrafish are diurnal; when we look at the total number of observations of sleep and wake, we can see that most sleep tends to occur during the night and most wake occurs during the day.

```{r Section 5.1}
total_counts_plot <- ggplot(fish_WT, aes(x = ___, fill = state)) 

total_counts_plot <- total_counts_plot + annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 9, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey", alpha = 0.6) + annotate("rect", xmin = 22.0, xmax = 23.9, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey", alpha = 0.6) 

total_counts_plot <- total_counts_plot + geom_histogram(colour = "black", bins = 25) 

total_counts_plot <- total_counts_plot + scale_fill_manual(values = c("slateblue4", "lightseagreen" )) 

total_counts_plot <- total_counts_plot + ggtitle("Plot 5: Total wake vs sleep observations in day vs night")

total_counts_plot
```

## Section 6: Comparison of sleep cycles in hypocretin knockouts vs wildtype

We want to compare the proportion of time sleep awake and the proportion of time spent asleep in the wildtype individuals vs the hypocretin knockouts.

To do this, we can use the count() function to count the number of observations for each state (wake vs sleep) in each hour (0-23) for each genotype (wildtype, homozygous KO, heterozygous KO). This create a new datafrom with a column called n which contains the counts for each group.

```{r Section 6.1}
fish_counts <- fish_df %>% count(hour, state, ___)

head(fish_counts)
```

We now need to get the total number of sleep and wake observations in each genotype in each hour in order to later calculate the proportion of time spent in sleep and wake out of the total time observed. To do this we select the columns we need, then we group by only hour and genotype. This pools both the sleep and wake observations for each hour and each genotype. We can then sum together all the sleep and wake observations using mutate and the sum function. We then divide the number of sleep and wake observations by the total number of observations to get the proportions.

```{r Section 6.2}
fish_counts <- fish_counts %>% select(hour, state, genotype, n) %>% group_by(___, ___) %>% mutate(totals = sum(n))

fish_counts$proportions <- fish_counts$n/fish_counts$totals

head(fish_counts)
```

We can now plot the proportion of total time spent in sleep and wake for each genotype over 24 hours.

```{r Section 6.3}
proportion_plot <- ggplot(fish_counts, aes(x = hour, y = ___, color = genotype)) 

proportion_plot <- proportion_plot + annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 9, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey", alpha = 0.6) + annotate("rect", xmin = 23, xmax = 24, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey", alpha = 0.6) 

proportion_plot <- proportion_plot + geom_point()

proportion_plot <- proportion_plot + geom_line() 

proportion_plot <- proportion_plot + facet_wrap(~state)

proportion_plot <- proportion_plot + ggtitle("Plot 6: Sleep and wake proportions in wildtype vs knockouts")

proportion_plot
```

The homozygous hypocretin knockouts have more daytime sleep than wild type, the same result as we see in the paper. ![figure 1b.](zebrafish_figure_3_edited.png)

When we look at the total counts (not the proportion) we can see the same result. There are more sleep observations in the daytime for the homozygous mutants compared to wildtype.

```{r Section 6.4}
genotype_counts_plot <- ggplot(fish_df, aes(x = hour, fill = state)) 

genotype_counts_plot <- genotype_counts_plot + annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 9, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey", alpha = 0.6) + annotate("rect", xmin = 22.0, xmax = 23.9, ymin = 0, ymax = Inf, fill = "grey", alpha = 0.6)

genotype_counts_plot <- genotype_counts_plot + geom_histogram(colour = "black", bins = 25) 

genotype_counts_plot <- genotype_counts_plot + scale_fill_manual(values = c("slateblue4", "lightseagreen" )) 

genotype_counts_plot <- genotype_counts_plot + facet_wrap(~___)

genotype_counts_plot <- genotype_counts_plot + ggtitle("Plot 7: Total wake vs sleep observations in day vs night by genotype")

genotype_counts_plot
```

We can summarize this result with boxplots and use a t test to determine if there is a statistically significant difference between the mean of each group.

First we will plot the observations from the daytime hours.

```{r Section 6.5}
daytime_boxplot <- fish_counts %>% filter(hour %in% c(9:23), genotype %in% c("WT", "Hom"))  %>% ggplot(., aes(x = state, y = ___, color = genotype)) 

daytime_boxplot <- daytime_boxplot + geom_boxplot()

daytime_boxplot <- daytime_boxplot + scale_colour_manual(values = c("#F8766D" , "#619CFF")) 

daytime_boxplot <- daytime_boxplot + stat_compare_means(method = "t.test")

daytime_boxplot <- daytime_boxplot + ggtitle("Plot 8: Sleep and wake observations in wildtype and knockouts during the day") 

daytime_boxplot

```
Next we will plot the observations from the nighttime hours.

```{r Section 6.6}
nighttime_boxplot <- fish_counts %>% filter(hour %in% ___, genotype %in% c("WT", "Hom"))  %>% ggplot(., aes(x = state, y = proportions, color = genotype)) 

nighttime_boxplot <- nighttime_boxplot + geom_boxplot() 

nighttime_boxplot <- nighttime_boxplot + scale_colour_manual(values = c("#F8766D" , "#619CFF")) 

nighttime_boxplot <- nighttime_boxplot + stat_compare_means(method = "t.test")

nighttime_boxplot <- nighttime_boxplot + ggtitle("Plot 9: Sleep and wake observations in wildtype and knockouts during the night")

nighttime_boxplot
```
We can see there is a statistically significant effect only during the ___ and not the ___.
The statistically significant effect is an ___ in sleep in the ___ genotype, p value = ___.
